source.name: OER Commons open sales & customer success curriculum

course.title: Sales & Customer Success
course.description: A practical, consultative walk through the whole revenue lifecycle — from earning a buyer's trust and running honest discovery to closing fairly, handing off cleanly, and keeping customers so they renew and grow. Structure adapted from open sales and customer-success curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: The healthiest way to think about modern selling is…
options: convincing people to buy things they do not need
helping the right buyer reach a good decision
winning every deal regardless of fit
talking more than the buyer does
questions.explanation: Consultative selling starts from fit and value, not pressure — see 'The modern sales mindset'.

questions.prompt: In the BANT framework, the 'A' stands for…
questions.explanation: BANT is Budget, Authority, Need, and Timeline — Authority is whether your contact can decide or influence the decision.

questions.prompt: During discovery, the salesperson should mostly…
questions.explanation: Discovery is about understanding the buyer's situation through good questions before proposing anything.

questions.prompt: A fair response to a real objection is to…
options: acknowledge it, understand it, then address it
tell the buyer they are wrong
questions.explanation: Objections are information; you surface the concern, confirm it, and respond honestly.

questions.prompt: Customer churn refers to…
options: customers who stop paying or leave
questions.explanation: Churn is the loss of customers or revenue over a period — the opposite of retention.

questions.prompt: Net Revenue Retention (NRR) above 100 percent means…
options: the company lost revenue from existing customers
existing customers grew in value even after churn
questions.explanation: NRR over 100 percent means expansion from existing customers outweighed churn and contraction.

questions.prompt: The handoff from sales to onboarding matters because…
options: it lets sales forget the customer
a clean transfer of context sets up early success
it delays the customer's first value
onboarding does not need any background
questions.explanation: Passing along goals, expectations, and context prevents the customer from repeating themselves and speeds time-to-value.

questions.prompt: Comparing CAC and LTV tells you…
options: whether acquiring a customer pays off over time
questions.explanation: Customer Acquisition Cost versus Lifetime Value shows whether the economics of winning a customer are sustainable.

lessons.title: The modern sales mindset: value, not pressure
lessons.grammar_note: Consultative selling means you diagnose before you prescribe — like a good doctor, you earn the right to recommend by first understanding the problem.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe selling as a service to the buyer, tell the difference between consultative and pressure-based approaches, and explain why fit beats force. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is the healthiest way to think about modern selling?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Selling is helping the right person make a good decision about a real problem. The old caricature of sales — pushing, manipulating, closing at any cost — is not only unethical, it performs worse over time, because buyers remember how they were treated and word travels. A consultative seller works like a trusted advisor: understand the buyer's situation, judge honestly whether your offering fits, and if it does, make the value concrete. If it does not fit, say so; walking away from a bad-fit deal protects your reputation and your customer-success team from a customer who will churn angrily. Value is the difference between what a solution is worth to the buyer and what it costs them. Your job is to help the buyer see that value clearly and truthfully, not to inflate it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Two sellers meet the same buyer who runs a small clinic drowning in paperwork. The pressure seller opens with a discount deadline and a demo of every feature. The consultative seller asks what the paperwork costs the clinic in hours and errors, learns that staff burnout is the real pain, and then shows only the two features that cut that burden — framing the price against the hours saved each week. The second seller closes fewer but healthier deals: customers who bought for a reason they can name, who onboard smoothly, and who renew. Fit-first selling trades a little short-term volume for durable revenue and referrals.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what does a consultative seller do before recommending anything? 2) Why can walking away from a bad-fit deal be the right call? 3) Define 'value' in a buyer's terms. 4) Name one long-term cost of pressure tactics. 5) True or false: closing more deals always means a healthier business. Answers: 1) They diagnose the buyer's situation and problem. 2) A poor fit tends to churn, complain, and damage your reputation, costing more than the deal is worth. 3) Value is what the solution is worth to the buyer minus what it costs them. 4) Lost trust, bad word of mouth, higher churn, or refunds. 5) False — deals that do not fit can raise churn and support costs and hurt the brand.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: leading with features and price before understanding the problem. Mistake: treating every prospect as a deal to be won rather than a decision to be helped. Exit: (a) What is the core question a consultative seller tries to answer about fit? (b) Name one reason fit-first selling produces healthier revenue. Answers: whether the offering genuinely solves this buyer's problem; it yields customers who onboard well, renew, and refer, lowering churn and support cost.

lessons.title: Understanding buyers and the buying journey
lessons.grammar_note: Buyers move through awareness, consideration, and decision stages — meet them where they are, and do not pitch a decision-stage offer to someone still defining their problem.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Map the stages a buyer moves through, tell the difference between a buyer's job and their emotions, and match your message to the stage they are in. Warm-up: should you send a pricing quote to someone who has not yet decided they have a problem?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: People rarely buy on a whim in business. They move through a journey: awareness (I have a problem or goal), consideration (what are my options?), and decision (which option, and can I justify it?). At each stage the buyer needs something different — education early, comparison in the middle, and reassurance and proof at the end. There is often more than one person involved: an economic buyer who controls budget, a champion who advocates internally, users who live with the tool, and sometimes a blocker who resists change. Buyers also carry emotions — fear of making a costly mistake, hope of looking smart, pressure from their own boss. Good sellers address both the rational job to be done and the human feelings around the decision.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A buyer researching scheduling software first reads a blog post about reducing no-shows (awareness). Weeks later they compare three vendors on a spreadsheet (consideration). Finally they need a reference customer and a clear rollout plan to convince their manager (decision). A seller who sends a hard-close email during the awareness stage feels pushy and gets ignored; the same email at the decision stage feels helpful. Meanwhile the office manager is the daily user, but the practice owner signs the check — so the seller earns the office manager as a champion and gives the owner the numbers that justify the spend.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three broad stages of the buying journey. 2) What does a buyer mainly need in the consideration stage? 3) Who is the 'economic buyer'? 4) Give one emotion a buyer might feel near a big decision. 5) Why identify a champion? Answers: 1) Awareness, consideration, and decision. 2) Comparison — help weighing options against each other. 3) The person who controls the budget and approves the spend. 4) Fear of a costly mistake, hope of looking capable, or pressure from above. 5) A champion advocates for your solution inside the buyer's organization when you are not in the room.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: pitching a decision-stage offer to an awareness-stage buyer. Mistake: talking only to the user and forgetting who signs, or only to the signer and ignoring the daily user. Exit: (a) Match this message to a stage: 'Here is a checklist of what to look for when comparing vendors.' (b) Why involve both a champion and the economic buyer? Answers: consideration stage; the champion drives the deal internally while the economic buyer must be given the justification to approve budget.

lessons.title: Prospecting and qualifying leads: BANT and MEDDIC basics
lessons.grammar_note: Qualifying is not gatekeeping people out; it is spending your limited time where you can genuinely help — a poorly qualified pipeline wastes both sides' time.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what prospecting and qualifying are, and use two common frameworks — BANT and MEDDIC — to judge whether a lead is worth pursuing. Warm-up: what does the 'A' in BANT stand for?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Prospecting is finding people who might benefit from what you offer; qualifying is deciding, respectfully, whether pursuing a given lead is a good use of everyone's time. BANT is a simple checklist: Budget (can they fund a solution?), Authority (is your contact a decision-maker or influencer?), Need (is there a real problem you solve?), and Timeline (when do they intend to act?). MEDDIC goes deeper for complex deals: Metrics (the measurable impact they want), Economic buyer (who signs), Decision criteria (how they will judge options), Decision process (the steps and approvals), Identify pain (the concrete problem), and Champion (an internal advocate). Neither framework is a script to interrogate people with; they are reminders of what you still need to learn. A lead that fails a criterion is not a failure — it is a signal to nurture for later or to move on kindly.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A seller gets an inbound demo request. Using BANT in a friendly first call, they learn there is a clear Need and a Timeline of this quarter, but the contact lacks Authority and no Budget is set aside. Rather than force a demo, the seller helps the contact build an internal case and get the economic buyer on the next call — turning a weak lead into a qualified one. For a larger, multi-department deal, they switch to MEDDIC: they pin down the Metric that matters (cut onboarding time by 30 percent), confirm the Economic buyer, learn the Decision criteria and Process, name the Pain, and cultivate a Champion. The extra rigor prevents a 'happy ears' forecast where a friendly conversation is mistaken for a real commitment.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Spell out what each letter of BANT stands for. 2) What does the 'M' in MEDDIC most often refer to? 3) Is qualifying meant to push people away? 4) A contact has a real Need but no Authority — what is a good next step? 5) What risk does careful qualifying reduce in a forecast? Answers: 1) Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline. 2) Metrics — the measurable outcome the buyer wants. 3) No; it directs your time to where you can genuinely help and spares poor-fit buyers a wasted process. 4) Help them build the internal case and bring the decision-maker or economic buyer into the conversation. 5) It reduces 'happy ears' — overcounting friendly-but-uncommitted conversations as real deals.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a framework as an interrogation checklist instead of a guide to what you still need to understand. Mistake: forecasting a deal as likely when only Need is confirmed and Budget, Authority, or Timeline are unknown. Exit: (a) In MEDDIC, who is the 'Economic buyer'? (b) Why is a lead that fails one BANT criterion not necessarily lost? Answers: the person with budget authority who ultimately approves the purchase; it can be nurtured until the missing piece (budget, timing, or the right decision-maker) is in place.

questions.prompt: The best one-line summary of consultative selling is…
questions.explanation: You understand the problem before recommending a solution — see 'The modern sales mindset'.

questions.prompt: A buyer comparing three vendors on a spreadsheet is in which stage?
questions.explanation: Comparing options is the consideration stage of the buying journey.

questions.prompt: In BANT, 'Timeline' captures…
options: when the buyer intends to act
questions.explanation: Timeline is when the buyer plans to make a decision or go live.

questions.prompt: The role of an internal advocate for your solution is called a…
questions.explanation: A champion advocates for your solution inside the buyer's organization.

questions.prompt: A lead has a real need but no budget and no decision-maker engaged. The best move is to…
options: forecast it as a likely close
help build the internal case and involve the decision-maker
questions.explanation: Nurture it: help the contact make the case and bring in the economic buyer.

questions.prompt: 'Happy ears' in forecasting refers to…
options: mistaking friendly talk for real commitment
questions.explanation: It is overcounting warm-but-uncommitted conversations as real deals.

lessons.title: Discovery and asking good questions
lessons.grammar_note: Open questions (how, what, why) invite the buyer to explain; closed questions (yes/no) confirm details. Lead with open questions, then confirm with closed ones.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Run a discovery conversation that uncovers the real problem, its cost, and the desired outcome, using open questions and active listening. Warm-up: during discovery, should you mostly talk or mostly listen?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Discovery is the conversation where you learn enough to know whether and how you can help. Good discovery is mostly listening. Open questions — 'What made you start looking for a solution now?', 'How is this handled today?', 'What happens if nothing changes?' — invite the buyer to tell their story. You are trying to surface three things: the current situation, the pain or goal underneath it, and the impact if it is solved or ignored. A useful habit is to quantify: 'How many hours a week does that cost?' turns a vague complaint into a measurable case. Active listening means summarizing back what you heard — 'So if I understand right, the manual entry is costing about eight hours a week and causing billing errors?' — which confirms understanding and shows respect. Silence is a tool: after a good question, let the buyer think. Discovery is not a hidden pitch; it is honest curiosity in service of a good decision.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A seller resists the urge to demo and instead asks, 'Walk me through how your team schedules appointments today.' The buyer describes a paper calendar and frequent double-bookings. The seller asks, 'What do those double-bookings cost you?' and learns about lost revenue and frustrated patients. Then, 'If that were fixed, what would change for your staff?' The buyer, now doing most of the talking, articulates the value themselves. By the end the seller can summarize the pain, its cost, and the goal — and only then decides which two features to show. The buyer feels understood rather than sold to, and the eventual proposal writes itself from the buyer's own words.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Rewrite the closed question 'Do you have scheduling problems?' as an open question. 2) Name the three things discovery tries to surface. 3) What does 'active listening' look like in one sentence? 4) Why quantify the buyer's pain? 5) Why is silence after a question useful? Answers: 1) For example, 'How does your team handle scheduling today?' or 'What challenges come up with scheduling?' 2) The current situation, the underlying pain or goal, and the impact of solving or ignoring it. 3) Summarizing back what the buyer said to confirm you understood it. 4) A number turns a vague complaint into a measurable business case and makes value concrete. 5) It gives the buyer room to think and often surfaces the deeper issue they had not yet said aloud.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: turning discovery into a disguised product pitch instead of genuine inquiry. Mistake: asking only closed questions, which get short answers and miss the story. Exit: (a) Which kind of question invites the buyer to explain — open or closed? (b) Give one benefit of summarizing the buyer's answer back to them. Answers: open; it confirms your understanding, corrects any misread, and shows the buyer they were heard.

lessons.title: Presenting value and handling objections
lessons.grammar_note: Sell outcomes, not features. A feature is what the product does; the benefit is what it does for this buyer's specific problem.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Present a solution as outcomes tied to the buyer's own words, and handle objections honestly with a listen-confirm-respond approach. Warm-up: what is a fair way to respond to a real objection?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After discovery, presenting value means connecting your solution back to what the buyer told you. Translate features into benefits: not 'our tool has automated reminders' but 'automated reminders should cut the no-shows that are costing you those eight hours a week.' Show only what is relevant; a wall of features dilutes the message. Objections are not rejection — they are the buyer thinking out loud, and each one is a chance to build trust. A calm pattern helps: listen fully without interrupting, confirm you understand ('It sounds like the concern is the switching cost for your staff — is that right?'), then respond honestly with evidence or a plan. If an objection is valid and you cannot meet it, say so; false promises create churn and refunds later. Price objections often hide a value gap — the buyer does not yet see the return — so return to the numbers from discovery rather than simply discounting.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A buyer says, 'This seems expensive.' Instead of dropping the price, the seller responds, 'I understand — let's put it next to what the double-bookings cost. You mentioned about six hours a week and some lost visits; here is how the tool addresses that.' The objection turns into a value conversation. Another buyer worries about staff resisting a new system. The seller does not dismiss it; they confirm the concern and share a concrete onboarding plan and a reference customer of similar size. When a third buyer needs an integration the product genuinely lacks, the seller says so plainly and notes the workaround and roadmap — preserving trust and avoiding a deal that would have soured in month two.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Turn this feature into a benefit for a busy clinic: 'exports reports as spreadsheets.' 2) What are the three steps of the listen-confirm-respond pattern? 3) A price objection often signals what underlying gap? 4) What should you do when an objection is valid and you truly cannot meet it? 5) Why show only relevant features instead of all of them? Answers: 1) For example, 'You can hand your accountant a clean weekly report in seconds instead of retyping it, saving admin time.' 2) Listen fully, confirm you understood the concern, then respond honestly. 3) A value gap — the buyer does not yet see the return relative to the price. 4) Say so honestly, and offer any workaround or roadmap rather than making a false promise. 5) Relevant features keep the value clear; a flood of features dilutes the message and confuses the decision.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reflexively discounting at the first price objection instead of re-establishing value. Mistake: arguing with or dismissing an objection rather than confirming and addressing it. Exit: (a) A buyer says the product is too expensive; name a better first response than lowering the price. (b) Why be honest about a feature you lack? Answers: revisit the quantified value from discovery and weigh it against the cost; honesty prevents a mis-sold deal that would churn or demand a refund later, and protects your credibility.

lessons.title: Negotiation and closing ethically
lessons.grammar_note: Ethical closing asks for a decision the buyer is ready to make; it never manufactures fake urgency or scarcity to force a signature.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Negotiate toward a fair agreement and close by confirming a decision the buyer is ready for, without pressure or false urgency. Warm-up: what separates ethical urgency from manufactured pressure?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Negotiation is finding terms that work for both sides, not winning at the other's expense. Prepare by knowing your walk-away point and what you can trade — payment terms, scope, timeline, support level — rather than only price. When you must give, get: concede something in exchange for something, so discounts stay tied to value (a longer contract, a case study, a faster start). Closing is simply asking for the decision once the buyer has what they need to make it: 'Based on what we've covered, does it make sense to move forward this month?' Ethical urgency is real — a genuine deadline, a limited onboarding slot, a price that truly changes — while manufactured pressure invents scarcity to rush people. Avoid manipulative tactics entirely: no fake 'today only' deals, no exploiting anxieties. If the buyer needs more time or the fit is wrong, respect that; a pressured signature often becomes an early cancellation and a bad review.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A buyer asks for a 20 percent discount. Rather than a flat yes, the seller trades: 'I can get close to that if we move to an annual agreement and you're open to being a reference.' Both sides gain. When the buyer hesitates near the close, the seller does not invent a countdown; they ask, 'What would you still need to feel confident deciding?' and address the real gap — a security review. The deal closes a week later, cleanly, with a customer who feels respected rather than cornered. Contrast that with a rep who pushes a fake 'ends tonight' discount: the buyer signs, feels tricked, and cancels within the trial, costing more than the deal was worth.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name two things besides price you can trade in a negotiation. 2) What does 'when you give, get' mean? 3) Write an honest closing question. 4) Give an example of manufactured pressure to avoid. 5) Why can a pressured signature cost more than a lost deal? Answers: 1) Any two of: payment terms, contract length, scope, timeline, support level, or a reference or case study. 2) Tie every concession to something in return so discounts remain linked to value. 3) For example, 'Given what we've discussed, are you ready to move forward this month?' 4) A fake 'today only' discount or invented scarcity meant to rush the decision. 5) It often leads to early cancellation, refunds, support burden, and negative word of mouth — more expensive than simply not closing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: conceding on price without getting anything in return, which trains buyers to expect more. Mistake: using invented deadlines or scarcity to force a signature. Exit: (a) Name one fair thing to ask for in exchange for a discount. (b) What is the difference between ethical urgency and manufactured pressure? Answers: a longer commitment, a reference, or a faster start date; ethical urgency reflects a real deadline or limited resource, while manufactured pressure invents scarcity to rush the buyer.

questions.prompt: During discovery you should rely most on…
questions.explanation: Open questions plus active listening surface the real problem and its cost.

questions.prompt: Summarizing a buyer's answer back to them mainly serves to…
questions.explanation: Active listening confirms you understood and lets the buyer correct you.

questions.prompt: Turning 'automated reminders' into 'fewer no-shows and eight hours saved a week' is an example of…
questions.explanation: You translate a feature into a benefit tied to the buyer's own numbers.

questions.prompt: A price objection most often signals that…
options: the buyer has no budget at all
the buyer does not yet see the value
questions.explanation: It usually reflects a value gap; revisit the quantified return before discounting.

questions.prompt: The principle 'when you give, get' means…
options: trade each concession for something in return
questions.explanation: Concessions stay tied to value, e.g. a discount for a longer contract or a reference.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of manufactured pressure to avoid?
options: asking if the buyer is ready to decide
questions.explanation: Inventing scarcity to rush a signature is manipulative and tends to backfire.

lessons.title: The handoff to onboarding
lessons.grammar_note: The handoff is a transfer of context, not just an account. Everything the buyer told sales should reach the team that will deliver the value.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Run a clean handoff from sales to onboarding so the customer keeps momentum and reaches first value fast. Warm-up: why does a clean handoff matter to the customer's early success?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The moment a deal closes, the customer's experience is fragile: they have spent money and now want proof they were right. A good handoff transfers everything sales learned — the goals, the metrics that matter, the champion and stakeholders, the timeline, and any promises made — to the onboarding or customer-success team. Without it, the customer is asked to re-explain themselves, promises get lost, and trust erodes in the first week. The aim is a fast, visible first value: the customer accomplishing the specific outcome they bought the product for. A brief internal handoff document plus a warm introduction ('You're in great hands with Priya, who will get you live') keeps the relationship continuous. Sales should not vanish at signature; a short overlap where the seller stays reachable reassures the customer that the person who made promises still stands behind them.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A seller closes the clinic deal and writes a two-paragraph handoff: the goal is to cut no-shows, the metric is appointments kept, the office manager is the champion, go-live is targeted for two weeks, and a security review was promised. The onboarding specialist reads it, greets the customer by referencing their exact goal, and skips the redundant questions — so the customer feels remembered. Within two weeks the clinic sends its first automated reminders and sees no-shows drop, hitting first value quickly. Compare a handoff-free transfer where the customer repeats their whole story to a stranger, a promised feature is forgotten, and go-live slips a month; the same customer starts their subscription frustrated.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name three things a handoff should transfer to the onboarding team. 2) What is 'first value' for a customer? 3) Why should sales not disappear the moment a deal closes? 4) What is the risk of a handoff-free transfer? 5) What is a warm introduction? Answers: 1) Any three of: the customer's goals, the key metric, the champion and stakeholders, the timeline, and any promises made. 2) The moment the customer first achieves the specific outcome they bought the product to get. 3) A short overlap reassures the customer and keeps promises accountable, protecting trust in the fragile early period. 4) The customer re-explains themselves, promises get lost, go-live slips, and early trust erodes. 5) A personal introduction of the onboarding owner that hands off the relationship instead of dropping the customer onto a stranger.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: closing the deal and vanishing, leaving the customer to start over with onboarding. Mistake: failing to record the promises made during the sale, so they never get delivered. Exit: (a) What is the single biggest goal of the first onboarding period? (b) Name one item that must survive the handoff. Answers: getting the customer to first value quickly; the customer's goal, the key metric, the champion, the timeline, or any promise made during the sale.

lessons.title: Customer success fundamentals: retention, expansion, churn
lessons.grammar_note: Retention is keeping customers, expansion is growing their value, and churn is losing them. Customer success is proactive — it acts before renewal, not at it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what customer success does, distinguish retention, expansion, and churn, and describe how proactive engagement protects revenue. Warm-up: what does customer churn mean?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Customer success is the practice of making sure customers actually achieve the outcome they bought — because a customer who succeeds renews, grows, and refers, while one who does not churns. Three ideas anchor the work. Retention is keeping customers over time, usually measured by how many stay from one period to the next. Expansion is growing an existing customer's value through upgrades, more seats, or added products — and expansion revenue is often cheaper to earn than net-new revenue. Churn is the loss of customers or revenue, and it comes in two forms: voluntary (they choose to leave, often from unrealized value) and involuntary (a failed payment). Customer success is proactive: it watches for early signals of trouble — low usage, an unaddressed complaint, a departed champion — and intervenes before renewal, rather than discovering a problem the day the contract ends. Regular check-ins tied to the customer's goals, not just the product, keep value visible.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A success manager notices the clinic's login activity dropped after the champion office manager went on leave. Instead of waiting for renewal, they reach out, re-train the covering staff, and re-establish the value — preventing a likely churn. Elsewhere, a customer using every seat and hitting limits is a natural expansion: the success manager suggests the next tier because it genuinely helps, not to hit a quota. A third account misses a renewal payment due to an expired card — involuntary churn — and a simple automated reminder recovers it. Each move protects revenue by focusing on whether the customer is getting what they came for.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what is the job of customer success? 2) Define retention, expansion, and churn. 3) What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary churn? 4) Give one early warning sign of a customer at risk. 5) Why is expansion revenue attractive? Answers: 1) To ensure customers achieve the outcome they bought, so they renew, grow, and refer. 2) Retention is keeping customers; expansion is growing their value; churn is losing customers or revenue. 3) Voluntary churn is a customer choosing to leave; involuntary churn is losing them to a failed payment or similar operational issue. 4) Falling usage, an unresolved complaint, or the loss of the internal champion. 5) It grows revenue from customers who already trust you and is usually cheaper to earn than acquiring new customers.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating customer success as reactive support that waits for tickets instead of watching leading signals. Mistake: pushing expansion that does not help the customer, which erodes trust. Exit: (a) Name the two kinds of churn. (b) Why is customer success considered proactive? Answers: voluntary and involuntary; it watches for early risk signals and intervenes before renewal rather than reacting at contract end.

lessons.title: Metrics: pipeline, conversion, NRR, and CAC/LTV
lessons.grammar_note: A metric is only useful if it changes a decision. Track the few numbers that tell you whether the business is healthy, and know what each one is really saying.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and interpret the core revenue metrics — pipeline, conversion rate, Net Revenue Retention, and the CAC-to-LTV relationship — and say what each one tells you. Warm-up: what does NRR above 100 percent mean?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Numbers keep selling honest. Pipeline is the total value of open opportunities weighted by stage — a forward look at what might close. Conversion rate is the share of items that move from one stage to the next, for example the percent of qualified leads that become customers; low conversion at a specific stage points to where the process leaks. Net Revenue Retention (NRR) measures how revenue from existing customers changes over a period, including expansion, contraction, and churn: above 100 percent means your current customers grew in value even after losses — a strong sign of product value. Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) is what it costs, all in, to win a customer; Lifetime Value (LTV) is the total profit you expect from that customer over the relationship. The ratio of LTV to CAC tells you whether acquisition pays off; a common healthy rule of thumb is LTV at least three times CAC, and you also watch how many months it takes to pay back CAC. No single number is the whole picture — read them together.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: A team sees pipeline looks large but conversion from 'qualified' to 'closed' is only 10 percent, far below earlier stages — so the leak is late-stage, perhaps weak closing or poor qualification, and they focus coaching there. Separately, their NRR is 115 percent: even with some churn, existing customers expanded, so growth is not solely dependent on new logos. Finally they compare economics: CAC is 1,000 dollars and LTV is 4,000 dollars, an LTV/CAC of 4 with an eight-month payback — healthy enough to invest more in acquisition. Had LTV been only 1,200 dollars, the same CAC would signal that they must either raise retention and expansion or lower acquisition cost before scaling spend.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does pipeline represent? 2) If 50 qualified leads produce 10 customers, what is the conversion rate? 3) What does NRR above 100 percent indicate? 4) Define CAC and LTV in one line each. 5) With CAC of 500 dollars and LTV of 2,000 dollars, what is the LTV/CAC ratio, and is it healthy by the common rule of thumb? Answers: 1) The total value of open opportunities, a forward look at potential revenue. 2) 10 / 50 = 20 percent. 3) Existing customers grew in value over the period even after churn and contraction. 4) CAC is the all-in cost to acquire a customer; LTV is the total expected profit from that customer over the relationship. 5) 2,000 / 500 = 4, which is at or above the common 3x guideline, so it is healthy.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: celebrating a large pipeline while ignoring where conversion leaks. Mistake: scaling acquisition spend when LTV/CAC or payback is unhealthy, which burns cash. Exit: (a) What does a low conversion rate at one specific stage tell you? (b) Roughly what LTV-to-CAC ratio is often considered healthy? Answers: it points to where the process leaks so you know where to improve; about three to one or higher.

questions.prompt: The main goal of the first onboarding period is to…
options: get the customer to first value quickly
questions.explanation: First value is the customer achieving the outcome they bought the product for.

questions.prompt: Involuntary churn is usually caused by…
options: an upsell to a higher tier
questions.explanation: Involuntary churn comes from operational issues like a failed payment, not a decision to leave.

questions.prompt: Expansion revenue is attractive because it…
options: grows value from customers who already trust you
questions.explanation: Growing existing accounts is usually cheaper than acquiring net-new customers.

questions.prompt: NRR of 115 percent tells you that…
options: existing customers grew in value even after churn
questions.explanation: Above 100 percent means expansion outweighed contraction and churn.

questions.prompt: If 40 qualified leads produce 8 customers, the conversion rate is…
questions.explanation: 8 / 40 = 20 percent.

questions.prompt: A commonly cited healthy LTV-to-CAC ratio is at least…
questions.explanation: LTV of roughly three times CAC or more is a common rule of thumb for healthy economics.

lessons.title: Capstone: build a simple sales and success playbook
lessons.grammar_note: A playbook writes down what good looks like at each stage so the whole team can repeat it — clear enough that a new hire could follow it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Assemble everything in this course into one short, usable playbook that carries a customer from first contact through renewal. Warm-up: name the stages a customer passes through, from prospecting to renewal.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Draft a one-page playbook for a product of your choice with these stages, one to three lines each: (1) Ideal customer and mindset — who you help and the consultative stance you take; (2) Prospecting and qualifying — where leads come from and your BANT or MEDDIC criteria; (3) Discovery — three open questions you always ask; (4) Presenting value and objections — how you translate features to outcomes and your listen-confirm-respond move for the two objections you hear most; (5) Negotiation and ethical close — what you can trade besides price and your honest closing question; (6) Handoff — the exact items you pass to onboarding; (7) Customer success — your first-value milestone and one early churn signal you will watch; (8) Metrics — the two or three numbers you will track and why. Write it so a new teammate could follow it.

sections.heading: A worked fragment (for a scheduling tool)
sections.text: Ideal customer and mindset: small clinics losing time to manual scheduling; we diagnose before we prescribe and decline poor-fit deals. Qualifying (BANT): confirm a named budget owner, a real no-show problem, and a go-live target this quarter. Discovery questions: 'How do you schedule today?', 'What do double-bookings cost you?', 'What changes for staff if this is fixed?' Value and objections: sell 'fewer no-shows, hours back' not 'reminders'; for 'too expensive,' revisit the hours saved; for 'staff will resist,' share an onboarding plan and a reference. Ethical close: trade a discount for an annual term or a reference; ask, 'Are you ready to move forward this month?' Handoff: pass the goal, the metric (appointments kept), the champion, the timeline, and any promise. Customer success: first value is the first week of automated reminders with no-shows dropping; watch for a usage drop after a champion leaves. Metrics: conversion from qualified to closed, NRR, and LTV/CAC. Use this as a model of depth and tone; build your own for a different product.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Write your one-line ideal-customer-and-mindset statement. 2) List three discovery questions you would always ask. 3) Name two things besides price you could trade at the close. 4) State one first-value milestone and one churn signal for your product. 5) Choose the two metrics you would track first and say why. Answers will vary; strong ones tie every stage back to the buyer's problem — for example: 1) a clear who-plus-consultative-stance sentence; 2) three open 'how/what' questions about the current situation, its cost, and the desired outcome; 3) any two of contract length, scope, timeline, support level, or a reference; 4) a concrete outcome the customer reaches early, plus a leading signal like falling usage or a lost champion; 5) usually a conversion metric to find process leaks and a retention metric such as NRR to confirm lasting value.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: every stage from prospecting to metrics is present; the mindset is consultative and fit-first with no manipulative tactics; discovery leads with open questions; value is framed as outcomes tied to the buyer's words; the close is honest with no manufactured urgency; the handoff lists concrete items; customer success names a first-value milestone and a churn signal; and you chose specific metrics with a reason. If all eight are true, you have a playbook a new teammate could actually run.

lessons.title: Final quiz: the full revenue lifecycle

questions.prompt: The core stance of consultative selling is to…
options: diagnose the problem before recommending a solution
questions.explanation: You earn the right to recommend by first understanding the buyer's problem and fit.

questions.prompt: A buyer reading an introductory blog post about a problem they just noticed is in which stage?
questions.explanation: First noticing a problem and learning about it is the awareness stage.

questions.prompt: In MEDDIC, the 'C' stands for…
questions.explanation: The Champion is the internal advocate who supports your solution.

questions.prompt: The best kind of question to open discovery is…
questions.explanation: Open questions invite the buyer to explain their situation and pain.

questions.prompt: Translating 'automated reminders' into 'fewer no-shows and hours saved' is…
questions.explanation: You connect a feature to the benefit in the buyer's own terms.

questions.prompt: The listen-confirm-respond pattern is used to…
questions.explanation: You listen fully, confirm the concern, then respond with honesty and evidence.

questions.prompt: Ethical closing means…
options: asking for a decision the buyer is ready to make
hiding what the product cannot do
questions.explanation: You ask for the decision once the buyer has what they need, without false pressure.

questions.prompt: The single most important item to carry across the sales-to-onboarding handoff is…
options: the customer's goal and the promises made
questions.explanation: Transferring goals, metrics, and promises lets onboarding drive fast first value.

questions.prompt: Voluntary churn most often comes from…
options: the customer not realizing the value they bought
questions.explanation: When customers do not achieve their outcome, they choose to leave — voluntary churn.

questions.prompt: NRR above 100 percent indicates…
options: existing customers grew in value even after churn
questions.explanation: Expansion from existing customers outweighed contraction and churn.

questions.prompt: If 60 qualified leads produce 12 customers, the conversion rate is…
questions.explanation: 12 / 60 = 20 percent.

questions.prompt: A commonly cited healthy relationship between LTV and CAC is…
options: LTV at least three times CAC
questions.explanation: LTV of roughly three times CAC or more signals sustainable acquisition economics.
